verdict.tagline: A sprawling tactical masterpiece that demands patience, cunning, and preparation.
for_you_if: you love deep, tactical turn-based combat
you want rich roleplaying with absolute freedom
you enjoy intricate character building and synergies

you dislike sudden difficulty spikes in late stages
you want a frictionless level progression curve

citations.review_text:
Came from BG3 and boy did i get humbled. 

Skill expression required from this game is less forgiving and really need to strategise well. The final boss fight is... interestingly frustrating lol.

But scratches the DND itch for sure
Everything is amazing up until Arx..   it feels like that entire final act was pulled from another game.  There's a difficulty cliff.. and the final fight is all kinds of BS.

A friend got laid with a female elf right in front of us.

Also, most of the combat felt like a chemistry class. Haven't finished the game yet (Arc 4 has a ridiculously steep difficulty spike).

10/10.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that the character building and classless system can feel opaque, confusing, or overwhelming for new players.

citations.review_text: This game is great and gives the player a ton of freedom in how they build their character. How to build your character can be a ambiguous/confusing at first since there's no set class paths, but the confusion doesn't prevent progress. Once I played for a while, the freedom of how to build your character and how your play made me love this game. 10/10
Really just an awesome game. Sheer number of choices and options can feel overwhelming but it's worth every bit of effort.

Amazingly good. Character building is a little opaque at first due to the classless system, and you're hand isn't held as much as you might be used to (quest descriptions in the journal could be spelled out a bit better as there's so much going on you tend to forget who wants what why). But overall I'm having at least as much fun as I did with BG3. The universe is more interesting, the story a bit more compelling, and the narrative and environment aren't bogged down with Wizards of the Coast's political baggage.

claims.claim: Maps become permanently inaccessible once a particular area is left behind.

citations.review_text:
**Bigger, better, deeper, tougher than the first instalment!!!**

Loved *Original Sin*, but its story threw me off. This one improves upon its predecessor while keeping the original formula intact. The combat is among the finest in the TBS genre, the characters are memorable and unique, and the presentation is flawless.

The game does have a few weak points, though. One is obviously the difficulty curve, and another is the fact that missing a couple of quests can be detrimental in the long run. Also, the maps become inaccessible once you leave a particular area.

A must-play if you love turn-based strategy games! Definitely worth a go even if you're new to the genre!!!

**Rating: 9/10!!!**

TL:DR;
What it is, and what it could be are two separate things that never met.
Pity, you buy it only to support Larian Studios.

Overall: 6.5/10
There are multiple issues that compound together to make this game annoying experience.

* First, maps. Pretty. Packed to the full with POIs. Every twenty steps or so is another POI, usually quest related. Overworld maps are very few, everything else happens in the dungeons or caves.
Which is... bad. There is no overworld travel, like in older Baldurs Gate and game is sorely missing for it.
Also you can't go back and revisit previous maps.
This together makes you unwiling to blindy explore and enjoy, because if you choose wrong dialogue, you miss on content.

* Story line. Confusing, as always in Divinity games. Has few decent moments, but other than these... it is very weak. 4 acts in total, you save the world from anihillation. Again. And Again. Character backstories are also very, very bad, as are their personalities. This applies to NPCs as well.
Whats up with this omnipresent annoying asshole syndrome?
Basically, once you max out the first playthrough, you don't have fun the second time. You don't want to know how the story will turn out for Beast if you didn't had him in a party during the first playthrough, because it does not matter - maybe one or two things will change in the end screen.

* Skills, combat, main enemies. Skills are limited both in selection and their range. 15m for a spell. Unless you stand on a high ground and it magically doubles. The problem? You never start on a high ground, enemies always do - and you are usually surrounded by them. So your first thing to do in any battle is to survive the first round and then close the distance.
Also skill levels and most importantly skill points and talents are very limited. At lvl 20 you are underpowered unless you collect a proper set of gear, but...

* Can't really craft or enchant your own gear. Only few makeshift items are available. …

claims.claim: Progression is tied heavily to character level, where fighting enemies slightly above the party's level leads to extreme difficulty or being unable to progress.

citations.review_text: Tried getting into it for the third time now but it is exhausting when I am constantly one level under par, and it is VERY important to be on par with the monster level in battles. I honestly figured this out from my first attempt trying to play this that the mechanics are pretty dumb its: farm levels until par with monster level and smash monsters easily. If not level then make it impossible to progress. This game makes me feel like I suck at games when the mechanic is stupid. Now in Arxs, I cant go back to nameless isle to do all the level 17 quests I apparently needed to do in order to kill anything in Arxs. I swear, every single battle in Arxs is such a pain just because I am one level under... and there are level 20! monsters here and I am level 17 soon 18. I just uninstalled it actually. Piss off!

I’m sure the game is perfect when played on Normal difficulty, but Tactician feels far too brutal and poorly balanced.

Difficulty and balance
Lots of bugs that wouldn’t matter on lower difficulties get annoying very fast on Tactician. The enemy often moves before you and one-shots your entire team with AoE spells, even when you have high Wits. Pre-buffing with Death Resist, Well Rested and so on should be optional min-maxing, not a requirement. I’m sure certain setups and builds make it easy, but then every fight feels like a cheese, and in a game like this you shouldn’t have to meta-game.

The last act is where the difficulty spikes way too much.

Exploration and quest guidance
Even if you search every nook and cranny, you might not find all the quests. You often walk into fights and get one-shot because you aren’t a high enough level, yet you’ve looked everywhere and there seem to be no other fights. Not exploring enough can snowball out of control, and you might end up soft-locked when it comes to power. Compared to BG3, which pushes you much more in the right direction with its quests.

Stat system
The stat system is also very unintuitive for new players. Why should my necromancer level Warfare to max for damage instead of Necromancy?

Overall
It’s still a fun game, and it’s fun to find strategies and reload until the AI’s RNG goes completely your way. Maybe its a skill issue, but I wasn't prepare for this to be as hard as it was for my first playthrough of a game like this.

With Divinity 3 on the way, I decided I wanted to finally play through the entire Divinity series so I could catch up and see where Larian came from before the next game. After playing Baldur’s Gate 3, which I consider Larian’s ultimate masterpiece, I was honestly expecting Divinity: Original Sin 2 to be an incredible experience, and to see where basically BG3 was made from. Instead, I came away pretty fucking disappointed. I can absolutely see why people praise this game. The world is beautiful, the writing has some great moments, the environmental interactions are creative, and there are a ridiculous number of systems to experiment with. But actually playing through it feels like a slow, exhausting slog. It constantly feels like I'm fighting the game's systems rather than enjoying the RPG underneath them. The biggest problem for me is progression. The game has this incredibly strict power curve where fighting enemies even slightly above your level can turn into a nightmare. So you need to level up before taking them on... but figuring out where you're supposed to level up becomes its own problem. You end up checking every building, talking to every NPC, searching every corner for quests and enemies that are actually appropriate for your level. There are even abilities that let you reveal hidden spirits and information, which sounds cool until you realize you're encouraged to constantly use them everywhere because you don't want to miss something important. It completely kills the feeling of simply exploring. Instead of thinking, "Where do I want to go?", I'm thinking, "Am I the correct level for this area?" It makes the world feel much more linear than it should, because wandering somewhere you're not supposed to be can get you absolutely destroyed. And then there's the Action Point system. citation.review_text: After playing Baldurs Gate 3 and Divinity Sin, i was very excited for that game. And it did not let me down. 141 hours of pure enjoment, spells, crazy enemies, confusing riddles, and tactical combat. Me and my Bro played that game on Tactician Mode and after the first 10 Hours i wanted to lower the difficulty, because we died a lot, but turns out its impossible to change difficulty. hahaha. so we had to fight our way through the game and i guess it all worked out. Probably took us around 5 Months to finish. Cant wait for the new Divinity coming one day. Its gonna be Peak.
